newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Beleaguered consumer to block U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Beleaguered consumer to block U.S. growth.

text.p: A near-term slowdown in consumer spending will apply the brakes to the long-running U.S. expansion, according to economists in a Reuters poll.

On average, 27 respondents to the Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey projected Gross Domestic Product growth declined to an annual rate of 2.1 percent in the third quarter of 1996 from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
After a brief pickup to 2.6 percent to close out 1996, GDP expansion will average about 2.0 percent or less through the second half of 1998, the experts projected.

"The question is, is the slowdown a third-quarter effect or will it continue," asked Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch Government Securities Inc. "We feel fundamentally it will continue, mostly because of the slowdown in consumer spending we're expecting."
Because consumer spending accounts for two-thirds or more of U.S. output, as the consumer goes, so goes the economy, agreed several pundits whose forecasts closely matched the consensus.

"We have consumer spending falling to about 0.5 percent in the third quarter, versus the over-3.0 percent rate we saw (in the second) quarter," said Katz. "We expect consumer spending to pick up a bit from that very modest pace, but not considerably."
While the experts cited various reasons for the drop in spending, most said the problem stems at least in part from the heady buildup of consumer credit in recent years.
"The consumer is getting to the maxed-out point with credit," said Kurt Karl, chief economist for U.S. forecasting at WEFA Group.

Institutions' willingness to grant credit swelled consumers' buying power but has led to more defaults and delinquencies. Consequently, some economists believe, installment debt has grown more slowly in recent months.
"We're going to have a slowdown in the consumer's ability to get credit and spend money," Karl predicted.
U.S. consumer installment credit grew by $3.3 billion in August, which the Federal Reserve said was the slowest monthly pace of credit growth since a contraction of $200 million in May 1993.
But a litmus test of consumers' willingness and ability to spend lurks only a couple of months away, economists said.

"The caution on the part of consumers to spend, if it's prolonged and goes through the Christmas season, will cause a retrenchment in retail and wholesale inventories ... and a reduction in production," said Philip Braverman, chief economist at DKB Securities (USA) Inc.
Braverman forecast GDP would expand at a rate between 1.5 and 1.8 percent over the next two years.
Other economic elements besides the consumer lend additional weight to the slower growth outlook, some economists said.
"We look for capital spending momentum to slow down and the housing sector, which was very robust in the first half of this year, to slow down," said Merrill Lynch's Katz.
Although nearly every survey respondent picked growth to be more sluggish over the next eight quarters, several economists said the slowdown would not be as pronounced as the consensus projection.

Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, forecast GDP would increase at a 3.7-percent rate this quarter and a 3.0-percent rate in early 1997. He agreed the consumer would decide much of GDP.
"This is another episode of consumers having bought a lot of merchandise over the past couple of months," Seto said. "They're staying home for a couple of months."
But because the pause in spending is "voluntary," spending will pick up again and revive GDP, Seto said.
